title: Reliable short-term forecasting of damaging earthquakes

concept.text: The innovation would provide reliable probabilities of damaging earthquakes before rupture begins, specifying where an event might occur, its magnitude range and the time window of elevated risk. A useful forecast would distinguish an approaching damaging rupture from fault activity that looks similar but does not culminate in such an event. Reliability would require both informative forecasts and calibrated probabilities: events assigned a given probability should occur at approximately that frequency across comparable forecasts.

The target is a prospective capability for natural earthquakes, rather than a retrospective explanation of an earthquake or a prediction of failure in a controlled laboratory apparatus. It is also distinct from earthquake early warning, which issues notifications after an earthquake has already started. Short-term forecasting need not promise an exact date or certainty; its central contribution would be scientifically justified advance probabilities precise enough to support useful decisions.

significance.text: Useful advance probabilities would create a major new capability for preparing for particular periods of elevated earthquake risk, complementing long-term hazard estimates and structural mitigation. The direct breakthrough would be actionable information before damaging rupture. This significance is a conditional inference from the forecasting challenge and the mitigation context described by USGS; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate that the capability has been achieved.

Conditional downstream possibilities include adjusting emergency readiness or temporarily changing operations where the expected benefit exceeds the disruption caused by an alert. Reduced casualties and damage would also depend on communication, construction, emergency planning and public response. Forecasting skill alone would not guarantee these outcomes, and false alarms, missed events and prolonged alerts could substantially limit practical value. These are impact considerations synthesized from the proposed capability, not measured benefits reported by the supplied laboratory study.

The laboratory result offers a reason to investigate advance forecasting, but its predictive success cannot be treated as an analogy establishing equivalent performance on natural faults. Predicting time to failure in a highly idealized experimental system does not establish the location, magnitude, timing or probability of a damaging natural earthquake. No historical comparison or quantitative estimate of societal benefit was supplied to support a more specific revolutionary-impact ranking.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is finding and observing physical information that consistently separates faults approaching damaging rupture from faults undergoing similar activity without a major earthquake. Apparent precursors can occur without a subsequent earthquake. The physical evolution of the precursory phase in natural, heterogeneous fault zones remains poorly understood and difficult to access. The supplied evidence leaves open whether sufficiently informative precursors exist for many natural earthquakes; it does not establish that they are impossible.

A successful method would have to connect observable signals to eventual rupture size as well as impending failure. It would also have to work when precursory seismicity is sparse and transfer beyond the idealized laboratory and numerical faults examined in the supplied study. Sensing, physical interpretation and statistical inference are therefore connected barriers: a model cannot reliably extract information that is absent from its observations, and a repeatable experimental signal may not remain informative under natural fault conditions.

As an engineering synthesis, the remaining task includes translating any informative signal into calibrated forecasts with defined geographic, temporal and magnitude boundaries. Evaluation must distinguish useful forecasting from chance successes, broad alerts and patterns recognized only after events occur. A method that performs well only in a narrow setting could still be valuable, but its operating limits would need to be explicit.

current_state.text: On October 30, 2025, Reiju Norisugi, Yoshihiro Kaneko and Bertrand Rouet-Leduc published “Machine learning predicts meter-scale laboratory earthquakes” in Nature Communications. They used acoustic-event catalog data to forecast time to laboratory failures in a meter-scale experiment. The reviewed article describes a chronological training, validation and test split, with 11 laboratory quakes in the held-out test segment. This is a limited experimental demonstration, not a prospective demonstration of forecasting damaging natural earthquakes.

The study reports poorer predictive performance when relatively few foreshocks precede a laboratory quake. Its discussion also emphasizes that the laboratory and numerical faults were highly idealized compared with natural faults. These findings support further investigation of fault conditions and precursory information, while leaving transfer to natural earthquakes unresolved. The small test set limits demonstrated breadth; it does not by itself show that the reported laboratory result is false.

A publisher correction dated February 2, 2026 states that the article’s originally published PDF was an uncorrected proof and was replaced with the corrected version. The notice does not identify substantive scientific changes. It therefore establishes a publishing-history correction without establishing either a retraction or invalidation of the findings.

The supplied USGS FAQ says major earthquakes cannot currently be predicted with the specified time, location and magnitude, and explains the possibility of scientifically grounded probabilistic forecasts. Its embedded related-FAQ excerpt distinguishes early warning as notification after an earthquake starts. However, the reviewed copy reports an update on November 4, 2026, after the review’s November 1 cutoff, so it cannot serve as a verified snapshot of USGS wording at that earlier date.

The supplied review assessed the retained article prose, including Methods, and the complete short correction notice; it did not inspect the main article’s figure images or supplementary files. The source index reports complete, untruncated text extractions without extraction issues, but the review supplies no freshness search establishing exhaustive coverage of the field through November 1, 2026. The dated laboratory demonstration and correction are supported within this record; the record is not a comprehensive survey of all subsequent developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: register forecasts before outcomes are known across several tectonic settings, specifying geographic areas, time windows, magnitude ranges and probabilities. Predefine the baseline forecasts, calibration and skill measures, thresholds for decision-relevant improvement, and the event sample or stopping rule. These are proposed criteria for making the goal testable, not an established consensus protocol reported by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: independent assessors should test whether the probabilities are calibrated and whether the method improves usefully over the predefined baselines. Assessment should include missed damaging events, false alarms, the duration of alerts and the population placed under alert. Forecast specificity and alert burden should be evaluated together, so that apparent success cannot be obtained simply by keeping large areas under warning for long periods.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed evaluation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should be able to reproduce the analysis from documented observations, forecast records and evaluation procedures, and confirm performance on additional prospective events. Results should state the tectonic settings, magnitude ranges, observation requirements and lead-time windows actually tested, including conditions under which performance deteriorates. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality across all earthquakes. Operational readiness would additionally require evidence that available lead times and alert burdens support the intended decisions.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: GEO-10, “Reliable transferable forecasting of volcanic eruptions,” is the closest conceptual parallel. Both seek prospective forecasts from observations of evolving geological systems and require calibration, useful lead time and transfer beyond a single setting. Their physical targets differ: GEO-01 concerns fault rupture, while GEO-10 concerns volcanic eruptions. Success in either would not establish success in the other.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-02, “A chemically and thermally resolved map of Earth’s deep interior,” could overlap through improved understanding of Earth structure and physical conditions, while GEO-08, “Establishing when and how sustained plate tectonics began,” concerns the historical origins of the tectonic system. Neither a deep-interior map nor a reconstruction of tectonic history would by itself supply a short-term forecast of a particular damaging rupture.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-03, “Geothermal reservoirs engineered economically in ordinary deep rock,” GEO-04, “Global-scale, verifiable mineral storage of carbon dioxide,” and GEO-06, “Discovery of globally consequential recoverable geological hydrogen,” share interests in subsurface characterization, geological variability and practical engineering. Earthquake-risk information could be relevant to some subsurface activities, but these entries retain distinct goals involving heat production, carbon storage and hydrogen resources. The supplied material establishes no dependency between their completion and reliable short-term earthquake forecasting.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-05, “Recovery of a detailed geological record of Earth’s first half-billion years,” and GEO-07, “Reconstructing the Moon-forming impact from independent geological evidence,” seek evidence about ancient events. GEO-01 instead seeks information available before future ruptures. All involve reasoning from incomplete geological observations, but reconstructing a past event and prospectively forecasting a future one require different demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-09, “Predictive laws linking erosion, sediment transport and landscape evolution,” overlaps in its ambition to produce transferable geological predictions. Its target is landscape change rather than damaging fault rupture. Operational earthquake forecasting and emergency management are additional adjacent activities: they provide forecasting and decision contexts, while early warning remains a separate capability triggered after rupture starts.

change_log.change: Preserved GEO-01 and its title while clarifying the target as prospective probabilistic forecasting before damaging natural rupture.
change_log.reason: The review distinguishes this capability from exact deterministic prediction, laboratory time-to-failure prediction and early warning after rupture begins.

change_log.change: Expanded the scientific barriers to include false precursors, uncertain precursory physics, eventual rupture size, sparse foreshocks and transfer from idealized faults.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why the laboratory demonstration does not complete the natural-earthquake goal without implying that informative precursors cannot exist.

change_log.change: Added the October 30, 2025 publication date, chronological data split and 11 held-out laboratory quakes.
change_log.reason: The review supplies concrete scope and quantitative evidence needed to interpret the experimental achievement.

unresolved_issues: Whether sufficiently informative and observable precursors exist for many damaging natural earthquakes remains unresolved.
Transfer from the meter-scale experiment to heterogeneous natural faults, including events with sparse precursory seismicity, has not been established by the supplied evidence.
The supplied record does not determine useful natural-earthquake lead times, achievable geographic or magnitude precision, or acceptable alert burdens.
Numerical calibration and skill thresholds, baseline choices, and the prospective event sample or stopping rule remain to be specified for any actual demonstration.
The correction notice does not enumerate differences between the uncorrected proof PDF and the replacement, so their scientific significance cannot be determined from the notice alone.
The review contains no freshness search establishing comprehensive field coverage through November 1, 2026; the USGS copy updated November 4 cannot resolve that earlier snapshot.
Main-article figure images and supplementary files were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting conclusions that would depend on those materials.
